name: Hirakud Dam
summary: A composite dam on the Mahanadi above Sambalpur, planned after the floods of 1937 and begun under the colonial government. Sir Hawthorne Lewis laid a foundation in 1946; Jawaharlal Nehru laid the first concrete in 1948; Odisha Hydro Power Corporation records the dam complete in August 1956 and Nehru’s inauguration on 13 January 1957. It was independent India’s first major multipurpose river-valley work, for flood control in the delta, irrigation, and hydropower at Burla and Chiplima. OHPC records Stage III, the seventh generating unit at Burla, complete on 13 September 1990.

Hindustan Times, citing the state government, gave 26,561 families from several districts, 325 villages, and about a lakh of people. Rehabilitation remained incomplete decades later; the National Human Rights Commission inquired into more than 26,000 families.

name: Bhakra-Nangal
summary: A concrete gravity dam on the Sutlej at the former village of Bhakra, with Nangal Dam, hydel channels, and canals downstream. Preliminary work began in 1946; construction of the high dam in 1948; Nehru dedicated it on 22 October 1963. The Right Bank Power House, five 120 MW units built with Soviet assistance, was commissioned in 1966–68. The project is run by the Bhakra Beas Management Board.

Andhra Pradesh irrigation records commencement in 1956 and completion in 1967; Indira Gandhi released water into the canals on 4 August 1967. name: Koyna Hydroelectric Project
summary: A rubble-concrete dam on the Koyna River in the Western Ghats, forming Shivasagar Lake. The hydroelectric project was approved in 1953 and construction began in 1954; the first generating units were commissioned in 1962. Stage III, a 320 MW underground tail-race station at Kolkewadi, put its first generator into service on 6 July 1975. The 1967 Koynanagar earthquake, widely discussed as reservoir-triggered, damaged the dam but did not breach it.

Construction of the arch dam is dated from 30 April 1969. The underground station at Moolamattom began generating on 4 October 1975; Indira Gandhi dedicated the project in February 1976. It remains Kerala’s principal hydropower storage.

name: Tehri Dam
summary: An earth-and-rockfill dam on the Bhagirathi, among the tallest of its type, built by THDC after a 1972 sanction and a 1978 start delayed by environment, seismic, and rehabilitation litigation. All four 250 MW units of Tehri HPP were synchronised in 2006–07. THDC declared commercial operation of Unit I of the 1,000 MW Tehri Pumped Storage Plant, using the Tehri and Koteshwar reservoirs, from 00:00 hours on 7 June 2025. The reservoir supplies irrigation and drinking water downstream, including to Delhi, and drowned Old Tehri town.

name: Sardar Sarovar
summary: A concrete gravity dam on the Narmada at Navagam, the terminal dam of the Narmada Valley scheme. Nehru laid the foundation on 5 April 1961; the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal awarded shares in 1979; construction of the dam proper began in 1987. The World Bank cancelled its loan in 1993 after the Morse review and the Narmada Bachao Andolan. The Supreme Court allowed staged raising of the height. Narendra Modi inaugurated the completed dam on 17 September 2017.

displacement.note: Who counted as a project-affected family, and at which dam height, was litigated for decades. Official NCA and state PAF lists and Narmada Bachao Andolan estimates have differed sharply; movement and commission documents speak of tens of thousands of families, many of them Adivasi, while canal-affected and other categories push some tallies much higher. This record does not choose a single household total.

name: Indira Gandhi Canal
summary: India’s longest canal, first the Rajasthan Canal, taking Sutlej–Beas water from Harike Barrage across the Thar. Govind Ballabh Pant laid the foundation on 31 March 1958. Stage I (feeder and main canal to Masitawali) was substantially complete in the mid-1980s, more than twenty years late; water reached the tail near Mohangarh, Jaisalmer, in 1987. It was renamed after Indira Gandhi in 1984. Stage II lift and distributary works continued toward 2010.

name: Kosi Project
summary: A barrage, embankments, and canal system on the Kosi under the 1954 India–Nepal agreement. Central Water Commission notes embankment work from January 1955, the Hanumansagar barrage completed in March 1963, and the Eastern Kosi Canal opened for irrigation on 9 July 1964. India WRIS dates barrage construction 1955–July 1963. The river is still called Bihar’s sorrow; the 2008 breach of the eastern embankment showed the limits of a barrage-and-levee design on a silt-laden, wandering stream.

summary: A composite dam on the Tungabhadra near Hosapete, a joint work of Hyderabad State and Madras Presidency whose foundation was laid on 28 February 1945. Masonry began on 15 April 1949; a major part of the dam was complete by mid-1953, when water first entered the canals. After States Reorganisation it became a Karnataka–Andhra Pradesh project under the Tungabhadra Board. It stores irrigation water for the Deccan and generates power at the dam toe and canal drops.

summary: A concrete gravity dam on the Narmada at Punasa, India’s largest reservoir by storage volume. Indira Gandhi laid the foundation on 23 October 1984; main dam construction started in 1992 under a Madhya Pradesh–NHPC joint venture (NHDC). Eight 125 MW units were commissioned by March 2005; the project is dated 31 May 2005. It regulates water for Omkareshwar, Maheshwar, and Sardar Sarovar downstream.

Manmohan Singh commissioned the 450 MW first stage on 10 October 2008; the second 450 MW stage was dedicated in 2015. Pakistan referred the design to a World Bank-appointed Neutral Expert under the Indus Waters Treaty; Raymond Lafitte’s 2007 determination required design changes but upheld gated spillways.

name: Damodar Valley Corporation
summary: Independent India’s first multipurpose river-valley corporation, modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority and established by Act of Parliament on 7 July 1948 after colonial surveys of Damodar floods. Four dams followed: Tilaiya (1953) and Maithon (1957) on the Barakar, Konar (1955), and Panchet (1959) on the Damodar, with Durgapur Barrage for canals. DVC later became as much a thermal generator as a flood-control agency. The first dam at Tilaiya is the opening date used here.

Cluster-8, a named satellite development of the same works, started production in April 2022 and was dedicated by petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri on 23 April 2022.

Construction of four deep-water berths began in 1952 and was completed in 1957; by 1959 the port was linked by metre-gauge railway to the north. India’s first export processing zone was set up beside it in 1965. It was later renamed Deendayal Port and remains a bulk and POL gateway.

It now diverts Yamuna water into the Western Yamuna Canal for Haryana and Delhi and the Eastern Yamuna Canal for Uttar Pradesh, under the 12 May 1994 sharing memorandum.
